utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we begin with the trial, if we can deal with one or two housekeeping matters. There are some exhibits here, Exhibit 258 and 380. They seem to be an identical statement of Witness MM-023, and therefore, they seem to be a duplication -- there seems to be a duplication there. I don't know whether maybe the registrar can correct this outside court and make sure that only one exhibit number is assigned to whatever of the two is picked up as the final exhibit. Maybe -- unless, Mr. Whiting, you have something to tell us about the two of them at this point, or do you want to look at them outside court, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, then. Maybe if you could look at them outside court and then make a report so that the Registry knows what to do. Okay? Now, there is also Exhibits 396 and 397. They also contain various pieces of evidence of Witness MM-044 which pieces of evidence seem to overlap, but they seem to be the same kind of statement also, excepting that the one statement seems, at least in the English version, very incomplete. It's got only one page in the English version - that's 397 - which is a translation of one page of the supplementary statement in B/C/S, but there are six separate B/C/S pages which I think are the main statements; the main statement and the supplementary. There is no English translation of those six pages. The further six pages attached to the B/C/S six pages are but pictures, emblems of badges of police and what have you. That's fine. But the first six pages are not translated. So if, again, Prosecution could look into that and give a report on what is supposed to happen there. It may very well be that the translation of the first six pages of the main statement were just overlooked maybe. Okay. Thank you very much. You may call your witness, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually Ms. Richterova will be handling the next witness and I promised that I would let her speak for herself today in all respects, but there is one housekeeping matter that we have to raise, and it requires us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. May the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The Defence has indicated that it intends to appeal the decision rendered by the Trial Chamber on Friday concerning the evidence of Milan Babic and its status. From my understanding of the Rules, and I just -- this will bear on the issue of timing, under Rule 73, the Defence has to get certification from the Trial Chamber in order to appeal, and the standard is set out in Rule 73(B), and that has to be done within seven days. We will oppose that. We don't think that certification is warranted in this case, that we don't believe that an immediate appeal of this issue is justified under the standard that is set out under the Rule. In any event, I think that's the starting point, is that that has to be done before anything else gets resolved. Perhaps we can talk about how that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me start with the first point you raised, Mr. Milovancevic. You raised first the point of the scheduling order and you say the Defence is going to file its submissions on that. I'm rather taken aback by that statement, that submissions are going to be filed on a decision, when, in fact, the decision does say that the scheduling of the case was discussed in court here, the Prosecution indicated its position, and the Defence did not say anything about the points. And that decision was made based on the fact that the Defence was sort of neutral to the whole thing. However, the only thing that I can say to you about that point is that the Bench will look at your submissions as and when it does see them and will decide accordingly. With regard to the next point that you made, deciding to appeal the decision of the Trial Chamber on the Babic statements, it's obviously your right to do so, and I'm again taken aback - and it may very well be here because of my ignorance of the Rules - that you stand up and ask the Court to stay certain orders that are made in the order pending your appeal. I would imagine that once you have appealed and the appeal is noted properly, whatever is in the order is stayed. So I'm not quite sure I understand your request to the Bench, to the Chamber, to stay certain time limits within that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure how specific I was. In your decision, you left the possibility for the parties to raise certain issues that were not dealt with during cross-examination and you set a time limit with respect to that and, of course, what I meant was the time limit would expire during the appeal proceeding. What I wanted to say was that we would act upon your decision concerning Babic's statements as soon as it becomes final. That is what I wanted to say, because of course we don't know what the outcome of our appeal against the decision would be. Therefore, the Defence ask that we be allowed the possibility that we do what you left to us as a possibility, even beyond the time limit of, I believe, seven days that you specified in the decision. That was the core of our application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the Defence cannot want to have its cake and eat it. You disagree with that order. Obviously you disagree with the time limits that are set in there because you don't want to go that route, and it is your right to appeal. Go ahead and appeal. Obviously, on appeal, if there are any time limits set in this order, and the appeal goes in a way that it feels it's got to make certain time limits, it will give you -- the Appeal Court will give you those limits. What you're saying to this Chamber is, look, you, Chamber, I don't agree with you, but just in case I fail in taking you on appeal, can you please keep the door open for me to come back in and carry out what you're ordering me to do in terms of this order that I don't recognise that I want to appeal against. You can't do that. It's a procedure that is unheard of in law and I don't think I can think of any rule here that provides for that. I think take the course you want to take and the Appeal Court will set new time limits. I would imagine. And -- or it will uphold your appeal, and obviously, when it does uphold your appeal, the time limits that we have made fall by the wayside with the order that falls by the wayside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one wrinkle and that is Rule 71 (B) and (C), and under that Rule, the decision about the appeal actually stays with the Trial Chamber for the time being because the Defence has seven days from the date of the decision to seek certification from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Whiting. I think they must set the motion -- why must they consult the Chamber for legal advice on how to do the appeal? They must do the appeal. Whatever way they want --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if the beginning, the starting point of that appeal, is getting certification, then they must get the ball rolling. We will look at that application for certification as it comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's due within seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They should know. That's all I say. Okay. I guess the Chamber is quite clear. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We understand you and that suffices. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That brings to the -- to an end the housekeeping matters? Nothing else from your side, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I would just raise one last thing on this issue, and that is because of the fact that we are approaching the end of the Prosecution case, I wonder if there is any possibility that the Defence could file its application under Rule 73(B) sooner than the seven days so that the Prosecution could respond and we could have a resolution of that perhaps even before the close of the Prosecution case. Because otherwise, it puts the Prosecution in a bit of a bind if that's not -- if that issue is not resolved before the close of the Prosecution case. So perhaps the Defence could be asked if it would be possible for them to file it sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, the body language that I read on my brother and sister seems to say that I must accede to your request. I'm disinclined to do so. I'll tell you why. I think it is that Defence's right to file the appeal, and if they file it -- if they can file it quicker, fine. It's just a request you're making, but I think any penalty they would suffer they would suffer if they fail to file within the seven days. And I would imagine that if as a result of the appeal, the Prosecution is not able to close its case because a decision has to be made on the Babic statement, then the Prosecution stays open. And if we have to go beyond the scheduling period that we have given, the scheduling order that we have made, so be it. There is nothing we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to be clear, I perfectly accept that the Trial Chamber -- I would not ask the Trial Chamber to order the Defence to file. I'm just asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- if it's possible. And I'm just hoping that we can stay to the schedule. And in the event the Trial Chamber denies certification of the appeal, then we would be able to stay with the schedule, but that will only be possible if we move quickly in the next 10 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in the event the Trial Chamber does grant the certification, then we stay out, I hear what you say. But to me, it does seem as if an appeal is going to cause a bit of an interruption in terms of time and we've got to be prepared to live with that to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If there is an appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I had thought that the primary stress would have been for the Defence to move for certification as a primary issue, before anything else. That would, in my opinion, be the greater concern because that is a hurdle which the Defence has to face.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: "Hurdle" may be a wrong word, but it's a process that the Defence has to face first, so I would think that they would proceed expeditiously and very quickly with that in order to permit the process of a fair and expeditious trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber can then determine the issue of certification and they know whether they are able to appeal or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. As a very last courtesy I will do to the Prosecution, Mr. Milovancevic, you heard Mr. Whiting asking the Bench if the Bench could ask the Defence if the Defence could be kind enough to apply for its certification sooner than seven days. If it is so possible, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I need to state my position now, Your Honour, or is it merely you conveying this suggestion to me? Am I supposed to state our position right now? I don't understand. Well, what I can tell you at this moment is that the Defence has always -- well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm merely passing the Prosecution's request. Not a suggestion, it's a request, and the Bench is neutral to that request at this stage. It says nothing to it. It doesn't endorse it, it doesn't deny it, it doesn't discourage it, it just passes it on. You decide what you want to do with it, okay? And you don't have to tell us your position on the request. I suggest that maybe you can communicate directly with your learned friend on that one. That should now bring to us the end of housekeeping matters. Ms. Richterova, the witness has been standing outside for so long.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go please to private session again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we please move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please read for yourself, look at the name, and confirm whether it is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can the usher please show this piece of paper to the Defence and Trial Chamber. Your Honour, may this sheet of paper with the name of the witness be admitted into evidence under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The sheet of paper containing the name and date of birth of the witness is admitted under seal. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 791, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to show the witness another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, did you provide a witness statement to the Office of the Prosecution on 6 and 9 November, 2000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On 30th of November, 2005, did you have an occasion to review this statement in the presence of an officer of the Court and did you sign a declaration attesting to its accuracy? The attestation is the last page of the document which is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness statement dated 6 and 9 November, 2000, was admitted into evidence under Rule 92 bis by the Trial Chamber's decision dated 16 of January, 2006. The statement was admitted in the redacted form, and it has been assigned Exhibit number 250, and I assume that it was done under seal. If the Registry please can check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the Registry please check whether the statement was admitted under seal as Exhibit 250.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the Prosecution indicated in its motion when requesting the admission of this statement, it indicated that there are certain matters which will be subjected to redaction and these matters should be heard viva voce. So my intention is to ask a few questions only based on these -- on the information which are covered -- which are redacted from the statement, which have been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand what you mean by "redacted" in this context. Do you mean edit or delete?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, we redacted from the witness statement and in fact we have hard copies of the statement which I would like to distribute in the court so Your Honours would see that on -- we redacted, based on the order of Your Honours, and what we suggested in our motion, we redacted certain parts from page 4, which went into the conduct of the accused. So we redacted this part from the statement and we stated that we would like to question the witness about this issue which were redacted, which means they are not in evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But now, if they are redacted, why do you want to question the witness about them?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Because by your decision, by Your Honours' decision dated 16 of January, the Defence counsel can -- it was ordered that this witness will appear for cross-examination on matters concerning Martic's Police or policemen or other SAO Krajina. This information is not in evidence, so the Defence counsel would cross-examine on something which haven't been covered in examination-in-chief or which hasn't been yet tendered into evidence. It's my understanding of the Rules. Maybe I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. I'm not even thinking of any Rule, but I'm trying to follow the logic of your discussion and I'm -- I'm losing you somewhere. This witness made a statement, okay? By an order of this Chamber, certain parts of that statement were deleted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, you want to lead this witness on those deleted parts?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then what would have been the sense of deleting them if you're going to lead the witness on those issues that have been deleted?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Because Rule 92 bis doesn't allow to tender into evidence statements which go into acts and conducts of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Okay. So you want to lead viva voce evidence on those to enable the Prosecution [sic] to cross-examine the witness on those points?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm sorry if I didn't express myself properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe the Bench -- at least, I'm slow on the uptake today. Thank you very much. You may lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before I go into these questions, there was only one small clarification which you -- when you read the statement yesterday, you stated that you found one small error regarding the -- that you stated that all the witness -- all the villages which are named in your statement, like Cerovljani, Bacin, Hrvatska Dubica, that they were part of municipality of Hrvatska Dubica. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were part of the municipality of Hrvatska Kostajnica. This is an error that I did not spot when I was reading the statement. Only after the war did they become the municipality of Bosanska Dubica, with the villages that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you say that they became part -- later became part of -- became part of municipality of Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hrvatska Dubica, Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just to assist Your Honours, the village of Hrvatska Dubica and town of Bosanska Dubica can be found in the atlas on the page 21, and it's grid 3D.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, in 1991, a certain part of the year 1991, were you still able to go to Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How far is Bosanska Dubica from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 200 or 300 metres. Only the river Una separates us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you went to Bosanska Dubica, at certain point, did you notice any men in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I saw one person in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification? You asked the witness at line -- I think line 5 of page 18 whether he was still able to go back to Bosanska Dubica. Then the next question is how far is Bosanska Dubica from your village. What is his village? I thought his village was Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please answer Your Honour's question? What is the name of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours will see it on the map, just under the name Dubica, without the word Hrvatska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under the name. It is there -- the name called Dubica, the area called Dubica across the river? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it the only occasion when you saw uniformed person in Dubica or were there more occasions when you saw people in uniforms in Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of uniform these men wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a camouflage uniform. It was more on the yellow side, and I had seen such uniforms on TV. I have a colour TV. It was similar to what the Serbian soldiers wore in Serbia, and I also had an occasion to see on TV the kind of uniform that policemen wore, the policemen that they -- that called themselves Martic's Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On this occasion, when you saw this person in uniform for the first time, did you know what unit or what kind of uniform it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you describe to someone what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. To my friends in Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what did you learn from them? Did they provide you any information regarding this type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When I described the uniform, they only told me that this was the kind of uniform worn by Martic's men, or Martic's Policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you, from these people, did you also obtain information maybe about when -- I'm sorry, where these people were trained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got information that they were trained in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When approximately it was in 1991 when you saw this -- this man in Bosanska Dubica, this uniformed man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in July, towards the end of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know Milan Martic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I only watched an interview with a journalist of the Croatian TV, I believe her family name is Herceg [phoen]. She came to Knin and I only remember one sentence uttered by Milan Martic, and that was, "While Mile Martic's foot is in Knin, Franjo Tudjman will never set his foot in Knin."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you learn from someone whether there were more Martic's men in Bosanska Dubica or in that area or whether this was just an exception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was an exception for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This man that you saw, did you learn from someone that there were Martic's men in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw just one person, and then from a conversation with my friends and from other sources, I heard that there were such men across the river in Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You already stated that you saw Milan Martic only on television, but did you learn whether Milan Martic ever come, or did you hear whether Milan Martic ever come to Bosanska or Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, we received information that Milan Martic could be found in Bosanska Dubica at a meeting with Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you learn from someone where these Martics came from, those who were in Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I apologise to my learned friend, Ms. Richterova, for the interruption but I believe that for the second time in her question, she is putting words into the witness's mouth. Just a while ago, my learned friend asked the witness about the people that he had seen. I did not intervene although the witness said that he only saw one person on one occasion. And again she is putting her question in plural. Can my learned friend be more precise in her questions and can she bear in mind that the witness said that he had seen only one person, and when she is putting questions to the witness, she should also mention that one person, not people, plural. That is the essence of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I can answer this. It is true that the witness said that he saw one person but he learned from, as he stated in his testimony, that he learned that there were more people who were called Martic's -- Marticevci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you show us where he said so?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm doing it right now. It is line -- it is page 19, line 19: "When I described the uniform, they only told me that this was the kind of uniform worn by Martic's men or Martic's Police." And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. You see now your current question is so far removed from that information that he received that it is very difficult to link, and you'd need to link it by asking -- by making a looping statement. At least to say to him that he told you that he had heard about what he says he had heard in line 19, and then ask whether those people he was talking to or anybody else told him what you are now trying to find out from him now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I may, on page 20, line 14: "I saw just one person, and then from a conversation with my friends and from other sources, I heard that there were -- there were such men -" plural - "across the river in Bosanska Dubica." It was the reason why I used plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. All I'm saying is that answer is so far removed to the question you're asking that that's why Mr. Milovancevic perhaps is still thinking of the one man he only saw. But Mr. Milovancevic, you see, we're being referred to two prior occasions where the witness referred to sources that told him that there were more than just one person. Are you okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, the instruction that you have just issued to my learned friend Richterova is enough for me and I believe that the issue has been resolved with that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Ms. Richterova. Just remember next time to establish a link in a similar situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you discussed this one man with your friends and you received information that they know that there were such men - men - in Bosanska Dubica, did you learn where these men, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in very specific terms. I only learned that they had come from the direction of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. It's concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the cross-examination will be led by my co-counsel, Mr. Nikola Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start with the cross-examination I would kindly ask the usher to distribute the witness's statement amongst the participants in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon. You have probably concluded that I am one of the Defence counsel for Milan Martic and that I will start the cross-examination as is stipulated by the Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the Defence counsel has just used the witness's full name, which the interpreter did not repeat in her interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, you heard that? You heard that, Mr. Perovic? Apparently you addressed the witness by his full name. Please remember this is a protected witness. We are in open session, aren't we? But then the interpreters say they didn't repeat the name, so that will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It will be in the original broadcasting because the broadcast is in three languages. So the original will be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So we need to delete it from the original?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French interpreters note that they repeated the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, can we make sure that both the B/C/S and the French interpretation and any other interpretation that is not English, that name is deleted. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Perovic. Just let's remember that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the warning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the future, I will address you as "Witness," and now I have a warning. I believe that the time in the courtroom is not right. It seems that the watch has stopped in the courtroom, just to avoid any delays in the future. I don't think it's showing the right time. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. I've been looking at it and wondering why time is taking so long to move. Thank you, we'll rely on the other watches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I shall now start the cross-examination according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Witness, since the two of us speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to make a short pause between my questions and your answers to help the interpreters do their job. In November 2000, you provided a statement to the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The statement has just been distributed. From your CV --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly go into private session? Because I'm going to put questions to the witness that might reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are in open session. You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You explained that in Dubica, there were 80 per cent Croats and 20 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was more or less the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In Hrvatska Dubica itself, Croats made a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a large majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you often travel to other places outside Hrvatska Dubica; to other parts of Croatia? And I'm specifically referring to the period after the conflict started, first the political conflicts and then the armed conflicts. In your statement you said that at that time, many roads were blocked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt? Two points, Mr. Perovic. Can I suggest that after you have asked the question, you switch off. That will force you to allow the witness to answer, but also the interpreters to interpret. I think you're moving a little too fast. Secondly, I'm not quite sure that the questions you've asked so far relate to Martic's Police. You've gone into a bit of background about this witness, which is what we should have done in private session, if we had to go into that background, and you had promised you were not going to go into his background. I'm not quite sure where else you want to go with your questions, and we want to make sure that the witness is protected. So we also want to make sure that you only cross-examine on the things for which you're entitled to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to slow down. As far as the questions I have put are concerned, they had to do with the dealings of this witness in a given territory, and they were to serve as an introduction to other matters including Martic's Police, and so on. First of all, I wanted to establish the witness's whereabouts at the time in order for me to proceed to the questions that should be the subject of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I'm saying is when you ask questions about his whereabouts, that's too close to home, too close to the bone, in terms of security. Therefore, we must go into private session if you must ask those questions at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we move into private session for the next couple of questions, and that will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, please try and give us the page references in the English also, if you can. In the statement, the paragraph reference, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the last two examples, the page referred to was the same in both the B/C/S and the English versions. And I will bear in mind the need to refer you to the appropriate page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before then, in Hrvatska Dubica, there had not been any armed Serb units but only the ZNG units, as you described them in your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that, there had been armed groups standing guard in the areas occupied by Serbs, in the areas where Serbs lived. I did not personally see them, but I heard of them. This was the reason why we started standing guard in our village, with the sole aim of protecting the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, that's to say in August, 1991, as you explained, most of the Croatian population, because of an offensive launched against Kostajnica, had moved out of Hrvatska Dubica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of them had moved out by then, but quite a few stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: With the Croatian population, did members of the ZNG move out as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They did. The last ZNG member left the area on the 13th of September, 1991. That's to say left Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After that, did members of Serb armed formations enter Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I heard, they entered the area on the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session for the next question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of your statement, you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Madam Nosworthy, I cannot meet your request now because I only know that the page in the B/C/S version is page 4. I really don't know what it is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, you state there that: "When most of the Croatian population left Hrvatska Dubica because of the offensive against Kostajnica, the SAO Krajina Police set up a police station in the municipal offices in the village. This was sometime in August, 1991. I don't know who the commander or who the members of this police station were." End of quotation. And these are your words, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This happened at the time of your departure from Dubica. For this reason, you don't know who the commander or police officers in the station were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says here that it was in August, and this is wrong. I must have made a mistake during or at the time when I was giving the statement because it was in the month of September that the police station was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it took place after you had left Dubica, and for this reason you were not aware of either the commander or the police staff at this particular station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite certain as to whether this was a police station or maybe a Territorial Defence Staff or anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer this with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were still in Dubica, there were no members of the Serb police there, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of the B/C/S version, and page 4 of the English version of your statement, you state, and I quote: "When the SAO Krajina was set up, we realised that many young Serbs had gone over to Bosanska Dubica and joined Martic's Police, known as the SAO Krajina Police." You also go on to say, or rather, you say, "when the SAO Krajina was formed." Which year did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You go on to state, "They were sent for training to Knin and returned as policemen to Bosanska Dubica." These are your words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, would that be a convenient time, now that that time is not to be relied upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hoping you would take care of the time because I could not rely on the watch. Yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. We will take a short break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, just as a reminder: In addition to having to switch off when you finish asking your question to allow the interpreters, there is also the all-important fact that this witness -- one of his protection measures involves voice distortion, so it is important that all mikes are off when he speaks. Okay? Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, my last question before the break was as follows: You spoke of young Serbs who were sent for training to Knin and returned from there to Bosanska Dubica as police officers. But let us first clarify. Bosanska Dubica is to be found in Bosnia-Herzegovina and not in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You go on to state: "The police officers of Serb ethnicity who served in other parts of Croatia left their posts and joined the SAO Krajina Police force under the command of Mr. Milan Martic which police force was called Martic's Police." In connection with this I have the following question: You told us a moment ago that you were living in Hrvatska Dubica and that you did not leave Hrvatska Dubica very often. How come you were able to know that police officers of Serb ethnicity who served in other parts of Croatia were joining Martic's Police and serving under Mr. Martic's command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received the information from friends and acquaintances. This was not firsthand knowledge, but hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You go on to state that you saw some of them in Bosanska Dubica but you did not know their names, which means basically you didn't know them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't know those police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You described their uniforms as light-green camouflage uniforms with bits of yellow in it. You also said that they wore berets with a badge of a double-headed eagle. Do you stand by this description of yours today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do stand by this description. The uniform I described I did not see. I stated that this was what I heard and I relayed it accurately. Therefore, I did not see the uniforms personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, you state, I quote: "I think a special police unit from Serbia wore these as their uniforms. I suspect that when the Martic's Police was formed, they were given the uniforms by this special unit." This was your statement. Now, my question is as follows: How were you able to know what sort of uniform special police units from Serbia wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I saw the Nis specials on television and that is what I assumed that the uniforms were the same, and this is what my assumption was based on. I did not see any of them in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the Nis unit. Are you referring to the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the police. I'm not a hundred per cent sure because I never saw those units personally and I didn't know who they belonged to. In my view, they were police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Another question with this regard: How do you know that these special police units from Serbia had given their uniforms to the Martic's Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I heard it. I did not see it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that you don't remember the insignia on those uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you don't remember whether they wore the police insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness. I don't have any other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this completes my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, there won't be any questions for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you two questions. In your written statement you described that around August, 1991, the SAO Krajina Police set up a police station and that both Serbs and Croats moved out of the village Hrvatska Dubica. Could you clarify who left the village, at what point in time, and why, in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, before that exodus, could you explain the composition of the population of Hrvatska Dubica and some other places? I would like to ask you also about Cerovljani, Zivaja, Slabinja, Bacin, and Bosanska Dubica. First Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sorry, I only want to know whether we are in private session because this information would -- I don't know whether we finished in private session or whether we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So this should be deleted from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. I'm sorry I wasn't alive to that. May we move into private session for the completion of this question, please. And may the answers that have been given thus far be deleted from the public record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber would like to take just this one opportunity to give, in a more -- slightly more elegant manner, the oral decision it gave a little earlier this afternoon on -- I beg your pardon. It's got to be in private session. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Richterova, next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Next witness will be handled by Ms. Valabhji. Therefore I would like to ask to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome, you're excused, Ms. Richterova. You are excused, you may leave the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls its next witness, Dr. Mladen Loncar, an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Mladen Loncar can be brought into court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji. I almost said Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, please state your name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Mladen Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, were you born in 1961 in Donji Gradac, Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Are you of Croatian nationality?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When you were less than a year old, did you and your family move to Ilok, Croatia, where you spent your childhood?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'd now like to read a brief summary of your educational background, and if you concur, please say so at the end. In 1987, you received a graduate degree in medicine in Novi Sad, Vojvodina. You then commenced a specialisation in neuropsychiatry which you had to interrupt due to war operations. You restarted that specialisation and graduated in Zagreb in 1998. In 1999, you completed a post-graduate study of social psychiatry at the medical school in Zagreb. You completed another master's degree in social psychiatry at the medical school of Zagreb University in 2003. Is this all correct, Dr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: In brief, can you tell us what social psychiatry is.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Social psychiatry is a branch of psychiatry that deals with problems of the health of individuals in community and the impact of that community on the individuals. That would be the long and the short of it, or in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you currently work as a psychiatrist in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. I worked at the clinical hospital centre, Zagreb, also known as Rebro.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I now have the assistance of the usher in distributing the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would the usher please help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you go on, Ms. Valabhji, that graduate degree in 1987, is it a first degree in the discipline or is it a post-graduate degree? Because "graduate" has two different senses in the American as against the English context, and I would like to know whether it's a first degree or a post-graduate degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, Dr. Loncar, you've been asked for some clarification. The degree that you received in 1987 in Novi Sad, Vojvodina, Her Honour would like to know whether that was a first degree or a post-graduate degree.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a regular degree after the undergraduate studies, after which I received the title of medical doctor, an MD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, you've just been given a document. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. This is my CV.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the document. I'm of course referring to page 2 of the English version. At the top of the page, it indicates that in 1999, you became a court-appointed expert in the field of medicine, psychiatry, appointed by the Zagreb county court. Was this appointment renewed in 2003 for another four years?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Once you become a forensic expert, this is extended every four years, providing that the expert has met the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, let's turn to page 6 of this document. At the top of the page, you mention your position as coordinator of the National Programme of Psychosocial Aid to the War Victims within the Ministry of Families, Veterans and Intergenerational Solidarity in Zagreb. Are you still coordinator of this programme today?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, within the Ministry for Families, Veterans and Intergenerational Solidarity there is a department for sociopsychological help that I'm in charge of, and the programme that you have just mentioned is the one that I am the leader of.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, is there anything else in your CV which you would like to add or change?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: As far as my education is concerned, there are several points that -- or several pieces of information that have not been included here, but it does not affect the overall information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 792, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, are you also the coordinator of the Medical Centre for Human Rights in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some more questions about the Medical Centre for Human Rights. First of all, when was it founded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: It was founded in 1992, and it was attached to the medical college in Zagreb, whereas in 1994, it gained the status of an NGO, non-governmental organisation, or a not-for-profit organisation, therefore a civic organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: That was actually going to be my next question. What does the work of the Medical Centre for Human Rights involve, in brief?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: It -- one has to emphasise that it was founded with a view to assisting war victims in providing them with psychosocial assistance, and also with conducting research into the health condition of the victims and into collecting information about the victims' experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, what is the methodology primarily used by the medical centre in relation to its work with war victims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The methodology that was used mostly, in addition to others, was the -- that of taking testimonies, or statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Approximately how many victims has the medical centre seen or treated since 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Somewhere between 4.500 to 5.000 victims, but not all of them went through this testimony-taking procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Those who didn't go through this procedure, was there another procedure that was used? How was it different?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: We applied short supportive psychotherapeutic techniques, or brief support, as we put it in psychiatry, and of course it depended on the victim involved, whether longer term or shorter term treatment was required. Secondly, psychosocial assistance in the general sense was provided, ranging from the provision of advice, counselling, and some other elements of social work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What made you decide to become involved in this area of work relating to war victims and victims of trauma?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The immediate thing that prompted me to work with the victims was the fact that I myself was a victim during the war. I had gone through several stages of torture, abuse, in Begejci, and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, when did this happen? Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Once a person goes through such an experience, one cannot become immune to that, and it simply forced me to work with people and help them, and that's what I proceeded to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And when did this happen to you? When did you go through this experience?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I went through the experience in the months of October and November, 1991, and I was then exchanged on the 10th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And after the 10th of November, 1991, were there any other incidents that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I must admit that my work with the victims was not that well received. My impression was that victims constituted a burden for society, and I came across quite a few difficulties through my work with victims and the protection of their rights and human rights in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Would you care to elaborate on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: In 1993, I experienced, I can safely say, something that was the bringing into the police station for a suspect interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you know why you were brought in?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The reason for that was - or at least this was the way it was presented to me - that I had to change some identity papers, but I knew that the main -- the real reason was my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And just so that we are all clear, your work being what exactly, at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: At that point in time, I was working on various projects, providing psychosocial aid and the protection of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to turn now to a different topic. Sir, were you asked to prepare an expert report in the case Prosecutor versus Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could Exhibit number 8 please be displayed. Its ERN is 03526654. Is it on the screen, Your Honours? Okay. I see it now. Thanks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Is this the expert report you prepared in relation to the Babic case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What is the focus of your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The focus of the report was the health condition, that's to say consequences, in some categories of victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the expert report of Dr. Mladen Loncar has been admitted into evidence in this case pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision of the 16th of January -- pardon me, the 13th of January, 2006, and it bears Exhibit number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, did you testify as an expert witness in the Babic case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And were you called as a witness by both the Prosecution and the Defence in that case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the transcripts of Dr. Loncar's testimony in the Babic case have also been admitted into evidence in this case pursuant to the same decision of the 13th of January, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: My next and last few questions concern statistics and information presented in your report. Let's turn to page 3 of your report, which is page 3 in the English and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it will assist: I happen to have hard copies of the report. If it's deemed useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, so far I've been able to get to page 3 on the electronic medium, so, being the least knowledgeable of computers on the Bench, I should imagine that my brother and sister are coping better than I am, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sir, on page 3 of the report - page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S - you address victims of incarceration. Now, paragraph 3 in the English commences as follows: "Between 650 and 700 non-Serbs were incarcerated in the Knin camps." Have you been able to locate that sentence, Dr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: My question is: What is the basis for this information, and what time period does it pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The information has to do with the period between 1991 and 1995, Your Honour. That is the period during which this approximate number of persons were in incarceration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the basis for the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis for the information, or the source of the information were the survivors, and their testimonies were taken in which they related their traumatic experience. Based on the information provided by the victims from these camps, we were able to reconstruct the number of persons incarcerated in those locations in the time period. Based on the victims' statements, we found out that these people did not only come from Croatia but also from Bosnia. Some of them were of Croat ethnicity, others of Muslim ethnicity. In their statements, victims pointed to at least two locations where the people were had -- held. One was the old hospital in Knin and the other was the southern -- or rather, northern camp where the people were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: As to the northern camp, the second one you mentioned, any idea where that was, from the information you've reviewed or that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Based on the information I received from survivors, these were camps held by military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, in this same paragraph, there is a reference to Martic's Police. And keeping this in mind, let's turn to page 12 of your report - which is page 15 in the B/C/S version - and on that page, crimes that occurred in October, 1991, in Hrvatska Kostajnica municipality, are addressed. At the top of page 12, and again at the bottom, references to Martic's Police are made. Have you located that in your report? It's on page 15.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What is the basis for this information?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: As stated here in one section where a survivor's statement is quoted, the uniformed persons styled themselves as Martic's Police. That was how they called themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm trying to follow your examination, Ms. Valabhji. I'm at page 12 of the report. I'm trying to look for the reference to Martic's Police at the top of page 12. You said to the witness both at the top and at the bottom of that page references are made to Martic's Police, and until I find that reference at the top, I'm not able to follow your question, "What is the basis for this information?"

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if you can refer us to a line.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The printout that I have - and I do hope that the page number corresponds to the document that is in e-court; I'm presuming that it does - it's the second line at the top of page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The second line at the top of page -- of my page 12 says, "Serbian forces at the same time took 30 more civilians from Bacin and 24 civilians from Dubica and Cerovljani villages to an unknown location and killed them."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I think I see the problem, Your Honour. I need to look at another printout because the printout that I have of this report is -- doesn't correspond in terms of the pages and lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the same problem as you do. In the B/C/S, the report is not numerated at all. And I have the same problem with the English version. This should really be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You'll take that into account, Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I think the version that's in e-court, Your Honour, it's at the bottom -- it starts at the bottom of page 11 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to help Mr. Milovancevic in the B/C/S? If you understand the language?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I have some difficulties in that regard, but I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I may give a suggestion. I don't know if it will assist. Perhaps my learned friend could give me the ERN number. There is always a page number, it's always the same for every page, and perhaps my learned friend could give me that reference. The marking in the top right-hand corner is always the same. Perhaps this should be used as a reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Actually, I think my learned friend read my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: The ERN in the B/C/S is 03526668. And in the B/C/S, it's the second paragraph and the second line of the second paragraph, which has the first reference to Martic's Police, in the region of this page. And the second reference -- the second reference is on the next page of the B/C/S, which is ERN 03526669.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found the text. I thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, and just so there is no confusion, in the English, it starts at the bottom of page 11, and the second reference is on page 12 in the last paragraph. I was actually looking at the filed version of the expert report, filed in February, 2005, last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncar, there are several references to Martic's Police in your report, and we have just looked at several of them, one being earlier on page 4 of the B/C/S, and the other ones being on the pages I've just mentioned. What is the basis for this information?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I received the information on the basis of my work with victims, who had on several occasions and at different points in time met persons who -- uniformed persons who introduced themselves as Martic's Police. That was the basis for their identification of these persons as Martic's Police and for their statements given to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to -- of course, my page references are a bit askew so I'll have to double-check this. It should be in the region of page 6 of the English, where the victims of displacement are addressed. And indeed it is page 6 of the English. And in the B/C/S, I believe the ERN is 03526660. Sir, on this page you address the victims of displacement, and in the third paragraph under heading 4, you state that tens of thousands of Croatians and non-Serbs were displaced or fled from the so-called Krajina SAO. Practically the entire non-Serbian population was deported, forcibly removed, or killed. What is the basis for this statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The information contained here stems from my work with victims who had been displaced -- expelled, either in the first or in the subsequent waves, when they came across the armed Serb forces, they managed to escape and told us how many people stayed behind. This was one source of information. The other was the 1991 census information. The assessment related here is based on these two particular references, and as far as I was able to see, we used sources of information by the UNHCR and others by the Republic of Croatia. Based on that, the assessment is that there was the total of 200.000 displaced persons during the war period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I -- I'm sorry, Doctor, you said, "The information contained here stems from my work with victims who had been displaced -- expelled either in the first or in the subsequent waves, when they came across the armed Serb forces, they managed to escape --" and this is where I want you to listen: "... they managed to escape and told us how many people stayed behind." Stayed behind where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, some people stayed behind in the occupied area, but this was just a handful, and most of them were elderly persons, infirm, who believed that nothing -- no harm would come to them. Based on my conversations with survivors, I learned that these people wanted to protect their property, their properties, and that was the choice they made, to stay behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you determined the number of displacements by subtracting the number of those who stayed behind from the census numbers of 1991? Is that how, more or less, in that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's correct, Your Honour. This was an attempt at reconstructing the numbers of people who stayed behind, the aim being to protect them. Because in the period between 1991 and 1995, we were receiving information that some of them had been killed, and with a view to protecting them, we tried to establish their numbers and whether they were still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. You may proceed, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually that was my last question. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Valabhji. I'm sorry I delayed you from sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: That's quite all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Loncar. I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Martic and my name is Predrag Milovancevic. We are about to start cross-examining you and we will be dealing with some issues that might be relevant for the Defence. Would you please be so kind as to make a break before answering my questions so that the interpreters could do their job properly. I will try to bear this in mind myself, and of course I thank you for doing the same.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we go into your background information, I wanted to ask you this: What was your task in these proceedings? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. At the request of the Prosecution, my task was to deal with the trauma of the civilian population and to provide an assessment of their health and the assessment of what they were through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Today, I have not heard a single word about the health condition of these people save for the fact that I heard that you counted the number of expelled refugees, that you know who the perpetrators of the crimes are, and I would like to know now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Just to point out that the expert report and the transcripts of his previous testimony, which discusses at length the medical conditions, the physical and the mental impact of victims of incarceration, victims of displacement, these are all set out in the admitted evidence in this case, therefore I did not go into it in great detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And your leading this afternoon was aimed at clarifying issues that the Prosecution thought needed clarifying? That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I elicited some background information on his educational experience, and then I focused on a few matters additionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, you may not have heard a word about the medical conditions of patients but you probably have read a lot about it from the witness's report, which is part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, your main task, therefore, was to analyse the psychological status of victims; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Psychological and physical and the consequences that the victims suffered. This is what my task was, or at least that's how I understood it, and this is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with that answer of yours, I would like to say that you are a Prosecution expert on the psychological status of the victims, or maybe also on the physical consequences.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a forensic expert, I can say that I deal with psychiatric issues. However, in my report, based on my education, I can also talk about physical consequences that the victims suffered, without going into any specialist field such as treatment or establishing diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since we have addressed this, you have dealt quite a lot with the physical consequences. Now you have just told us that you're not an expert on that. Does it mean that you went beyond your field of expertise in your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, in any case, as a doctor, psychiatrist, I have to refer to physical conditions or impairments suffered by the body in order to be able to assess a psychological situation. In other words, I did not dissociate the physical from the psychological, and as an expert witness, I can use the physical symptoms in order to present the consequences of war. As a doctor, I have general knowledge on general medicine. In order to become an MD, I had to learn about that and I had to be able to deal with those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get some clarification? From that answer you gave, do I understand you correctly to be saying that in fact the psychiatric conditions that you treat are induced by the physical suffering that the people have gone through, some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would therefore there be a relationship between psychiatric or psychological assessment and the physical trauma that a particular person may or may not have gone through? There is always that kind of relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for your question. Your question, as to whether there is an association -- and we are talking about trauma, it can be physical and psychological or psychological, and it is perceived as an integrity and we deal with integral consequences, bearing in mind which trauma was stronger, whether the physical trauma was stronger or, alternatively, whether the psychological trauma was stronger. Hence, the consequences will be reflected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. But there are some physical consequences.
