If I just look at some of the headings in your report, there are headings that dealt with victims of incarceration or consequences of incarceration, and then also displacement of people. Now, displacement of people and incarceration, this is a physical experience, and the psychiatric consequences or psychological consequences come after that, after either incarceration or displacement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Psychological consequences are usually prolonged and appear within the first six months, or a year at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's a different question or a question -- different issue. All I wanted to find out was whether there was or was there not a relationship between the physical and the psychiatric. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was your task also to establish, as a psychiatric expert, how many displaced persons there were, to deal with statistics, to deal with the 1991 census and similar things? Was that part and parcel of your task?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you are providing an expert report not of an individual but of a group suffering certain consequences, you can either do a case report and present it or you take a group of case reports and provide a general view of the consequences. I took the latter approach. I dealt with groups that suffered consequences, and I wanted to present the situation by groups and to tell the Trial Chamber what are the groups of persons that suffered traumatic experiences. And the second part where my expert knowledge comes into play is to show what the consequences were, in order to show the Trial Chamber what the relationship is between the causes and the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whatsoever in statistics?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I have not used any statistical methods here, and nor was there any need for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any experience in the legal shaping of statements and testimonies so as to make them credible in a trial? Do you have any experience as an investigative judge or an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that question a bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go back, we go on. I'm not quite sure I understand the relevance of that question, Mr. Milovancevic. Why must this witness necessarily have legal knowledge -- or experience in the legal shaping of statements or testimonies or be an investigative judge or an investigator? Now that we want to come back to the same question, I think I'd like to understand the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come back to that question later, but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. I have a prima facie view on this question that it is not relevant, and I've got to make up my mind whether to allow it or disallow it, and if I disallow it, then you're disallowed also in the future from coming back to it, so I would like to understand now what is the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you right away, Your Honour. On page 2, in chapter 2 -- or paragraph 2, of his expert's report in the Babic case, this is II, "The methodology of work with the victims of war," before paragraph 3, the title is "The method of taking statements," has a few goals, and the main ones are, number 1, research of violations of international human rights conventions. The statement was done as a legal document. In other words, this is the main characteristics in the -- in this expert's report when it comes to his work with victims. That's why I was curious to know, since the main task of his work as a psychiatrist is the violation of human rights, I wanted to know whether he has any legal knowledge, and since the statements were done as legal documents, I wanted to know whether he's an investigating judge or an investigator. But in principle, I wanted to know what his goals were, and I still haven't tackled that. My initial question was what his task was, what task was given by the Prosecutor as to what he was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All that long discussion and dissertation, you have still not given me the relevance of the question that says, "Do you have any experience in the legal shaping of statements?" What is the legal shaping of statements, Mr. Milovancevic, number 1, and testimonies? And whether -- and whether the witness has any experience as an investigative judge or an investigator? You haven't told me what is the relevance of that. Are you suggesting that this report that this witness has prepared as a report for this Court, is not a legal document? And if it is not a legal document, why would it be used in legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not suggesting that. Your Honour, I'm just checking the educational background of the witness and what his task was. He is here as a psychiatric expert, and I can see that in his report he says that he was involved in the legal shaping of documents. When he took statements from the victims, he shaped those statements as legal documents and he studied the violation of international conventions. And with this regard I asked him whether he is an expert in law, whether he's familiar with the job of a judge or an investigator, and this is a simple question. And my point is that if an expert, in his report, says that the method of his work was based on taking statements and shaping them as legal documents, I believe that my question was well in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't -- when you refer us to his report, I didn't hear you use the phrase "shaping documents into legal documents." In any case, so far as the witness's legal -- educational background is concerned, I think it's mentioned in his CV. That question that you put, namely the question that says, "Do you have any experience in the legal shaping of estimates and testimonies so as to make them credible in a trial? Do you have any experience as an investigative judge or an investigator?" And unless and until you tell us the relevance of that statement, or that question, that question is disallowed, and you may not return to it. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have gone past the time for breaking. It may very well be a convenient time to take the break. And maybe you can come back and carry on, Mr. Milovancevic. We'll take a short adjournment, Witness. We'll come back at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- quarter to 6.00? Yes, come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, on reflection, I'd like to ask you a question, maybe just to understand what you meant by that statement. There is probably a misunderstanding between the two of us on that statement. Are you able to venture an explanation of what you mean by that statement or why you asked the question in the manner in which you asked it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I assume that you're asking me about the situation with regard to the possible legal knowledge of the expert witness. Is that the topic that you're coming back to? I just want to see whether I understood you correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that it would be important to establish the area that the expert engaged in. Since it transpired from the examination-in-chief conducted by my learned friend that he was dealing with statistics, the number of population, establishing the number of refugees, expelled persons and the like, and in my view, this does not fall within his area of interest or expertise. He's not witnessing about any of that. He's not a fact witness and he's not testifying about any of that. And when it comes to the methodology that he applied in his work, I wanted to establish whether this had to do with something that has to do with his profession or it goes beyond his profession. If the expert is an expert on psychiatry, which we were able to establish from his CV, I wanted to know whether he has any legal knowledge, any legal education that is necessary for the job of an investigator or an investigating judge. When he explains the methodology that he applied as a psychiatrist, he says in this chapter that the main objectives of taking testimonies from the victims, the main goals that he had as a psychiatrist, was "to research violations of international human rights conventions - the statement was done as a legal document." And I quoted the expert himself. If the expert, as a psychiatrist, works on the violations of international human rights conventions and takes statements from his patients who have psychological problems, and shapes his -- those statements as legal documents, my question was whether he has any legal training to do that, and that was the sense of my question. I may have gone into great length just to prove that I did not have any intention to provoke the witness. I just wanted to establish what his area of expertise is and also what his educational background is. In any case, I was satisfied with his answer when he said that he did not have any legal knowledge and I was satisfied with that. We will come back to his expert report during the course of the cross-examination. And this is the gist of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The reason I'm coming back to the question is simply because I said to you unless you give me the relevance of the question, the question is disallowed, and you had indicated you were going to come back to it. And obviously if you have legitimate reasons for going back to it, it would be unfair for the Court to gag you, and then I just want to get a clear understanding why the question was asked. Now, again, I've tried to -- I want to understand what you are saying clearly. Obviously, statistics are taken by statisticians and are put in the proper --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for the interruption. We are not receiving any interpretation into B/C/S of your words. I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let's check out the interpretation before I proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it is okay. At least, I am receiving the interpretation in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. I was saying to you statistical information is put on the public domain by statisticians for use by other members of the community, including other professionals, so the fact that the witness uses statistical information does not make him a statistician because he did not compile the statistics. He went to the statistics that is already compiled and used it for his purposes. You now also refer to him investigating violations of human rights or international human rights conventions. Once again, human rights conventions are put there for people to observe, even people who are not necessarily lawyers. That is why people who are not lawyers get arrested and prosecuted if they break those conventions even though they are not lawyers. Now, I'm not quite clear, but you say -- unless you say that in those investigations of international human rights conventions, he makes legal conclusions in his report, if that's what you're saying, then I would understand you. Is that where you wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the answer would be only partially affirmative. In what sense? I'm trying to establish in my conversation with the witness what the essence of his job is as a psychiatrist, as opposed to his job as an expert psychiatrist. As a psychiatrist, he's a doctor who needs to help persons with certain health problems, and if that is indeed the case, and in his report he did speak about such people with such problems that were the result of a war trauma, then his main job has to be the job of a psychiatrist rather than taking statements and shaping them as legal documents, and I wanted to point towards certain direction, but in order to avoid any confusion, I heard your decision and I will not dwell upon this issue. If you wanted to know whether I'm going to insist on this question, I would like to say that I have to respect your decision and I was satisfied at the moment when the witness confirmed to me that he did not have any legal knowledge, which is also obvious from his CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that you had taken my decision but I reopened the discussion because I reflected on what took place before we went on the break and I want to make sure that the Chamber does not stop you from asking questions which you may be legitimately entitled to ask. This is the whole reason why I'm asking you the question. I want to be sure if the Chamber says it disallows a question, it understood your position clearly and that therefore the Chamber feels right in disallowing the question. And if it doesn't feel right, then it must allow the question. And hence I would like you to answer my question: Are you saying in those investigations of international human rights violations, is the witness making legal conclusions, in your view? If you say so, then that's the end of my inquiry. In other words, what I'm saying to you, Mr. Milovancevic, is are you saying, "Witness, why do you make legal conclusions if you are not a lawyer?" Is that the trend of questioning that you are going to follow? Or "If you make these legal conclusions, are you claiming to be an investigative judge?" Or -- is that what you're saying? And if that's what you're saying, then I understand exactly where you're going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm deeply thankful to you for raising this issue again, and for sharing your thoughts with me. What led me to put this question to the witness was -- I will put it in no uncertain terms now -- that his examination as a psychiatrist was from the start directed at establishing international human rights violations. In my belief, this cannot be his assignment. He can assist a patient, decide on a given treatment, and then, as a result of this, he can draw some conclusions on a given topic. Since here in his capacity as an expert, it was his mission to establish violations of human rights through his patients, in the context of what was Yugoslavia then, which could, of course, have been tainted by his impartiality for one or the other side. I wanted to show, by putting this question to him, that the course he took, if indeed that was the course that he took, was wrong and may have been open to impartiality. That was the basis for my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not sort of getting much further. The Chamber will lift the disallowance of that question and will allow you to ask the question, and it will stand, and you may come back to it later. The Chamber will be listening very carefully to your questions when you come back to it later to see whether they are permissible or not. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, in this trial, the Prosecution presented you as an expert who provided his expert opinion in the case versus Milan Babic. You looked at the document on the monitor and confirmed that Exhibit number 8 was indeed your expert opinion given in the Babic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please have a look at number -- at page number 1 of the expert report. I believe we have it on our monitors here. On page 1, Mr. Loncar, there is the ERN number 654 in the top right-hand corner, and the title is the Medical Centre for Human Rights. On the basis of this first page, I cannot conclude that this is your expert opinion given in the Babic case. You stated that you had given your opinion on the request of both the Prosecution and the Defence. Wouldn't you agree with me that the cover page should state: Expert witness Mr. So-and-so, the expert report such and such, produced on the request of the Defence and Prosecution in the Babic case? Don't you agree with me? And we can't see anything of the sort here.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the practice before this Tribunal is, what the legal procedure is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milovancevic please repeat the number of the page he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, will you please repeat the number of the page you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the monitor, we can see the page which has the last digits 654, and it's in the B/C/S, and we can see that this is chapter 1, the Medical Centre for Human Rights. I hope that this is the case in the English version as well, rather, that this is the first page of what is purported to be this expert's report in the Babic case. I would kindly ask the registrar to show us the last page. In the B/C/S it bears the last three -- the number 677 as the last three digits. I don't know what the page number in English is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. When I asked you to please repeat the number of the page you mentioned, it's because at page 70 of the transcript, line 7, 18.08 to 10, you said, "Could we please take a look at ..." and then the interpreter didn't hear what you said so it was not interpreted, and that is that page that I'm referring to, if it is a page. Or if it's a document, tell us. Can you finish that sentence, that's all I'm asking. The interpreter wants you to -- wants to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked of page 1, which has the title, "The Medical Centre for Human Rights" and the ERN number is 03526654. I believe we have cleared this up and now I would like us to take a look at the last page of the document. The page in the B/C/S bears the number 03526677. This is the document we received from the OTP. We are looking at the last page. Could we take a look at the one page before that one, the penultimate page, bearing the number ending in 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this the penultimate page of your report for the Babic case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We briefly took a look at the last page, which did not bear the reference of the case, the date, your name, your signature, or anything of the sort. On what basis should we identify this document, which was identified as Exhibit 8, as your expert report in the Babic case? This could be a press clipping. I mean no offence but I want to tell you that we don't have a single element identifying your report. Can I ask you, when was it that you produced this report for the Babic case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I produced it on the request of the Prosecutor's office, Your Honour, several years ago, when the trial proceedings against Mr. Babic were conducted here. I produced it several months ahead of trial, on the request of the OTP, and that is what it is, an expert report on victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have so far been able to see several expert findings, several expert reports, and they always bore the name of the author, Jozef Poje's expert report, Mr. Grujic's expert report, and so on and so forth. You are the next expert in line, but we don't have either a cover page or a date of production of the report, and so on and so forth. How can we identify this as a report of yours that you submitted before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I repeat, I produced the report on the request of both the Defence and the Prosecution. I filed it before the Trial Chamber, and I defended my report in cross-examination in the case against Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milovancevic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This expert report of yours, drafted for the Babic case, did it have anything preceding this page 1, like, for instance, an introduction, your CV, or, for instance, an explanation to the effect that this is the result of a request of the OTP or the Tribunal; anything that would identify it as yours?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, in addition to this document, there was another document, which was my CV, attached to it. There was another document, which was the written request from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the written request of the Prosecution a component part of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, it wasn't. The Prosecution told me to write an expert opinion of mine, and I did that. I repeat: Several years ago, I expounded my report before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You're telling us now that the expert report we have before us here is the expert report you produced in the Babic case on the request of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. On the request of the OTP and in agreement with the Defence in that case, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, we would find it very important to see what sort of request the Prosecution provided, in contrast to the one provided by the Defence. For instance, we don't have the date of the report, we don't have the author of the report. Can you assist us in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, for that matter, you will have to inquire with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you now why I put the question to you. Mr. Babic, as an accused, was outside the UNDU building in a private home, as designated by the Tribunal, between the 1st of December 2000 and -- 2003, and the 29th of June, 2004. During this period, he made a plea agreement with the Prosecution and it was apparently during this time that you produced your report. Did you see Mr. Babic at all?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: No. I only had contacts with his Defence. As for the facts concerning Mr. Babic's whereabouts and what he was doing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did his Defence tell you? Did they give you their assignment, and what was it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I did not receive any assignment from the Defence. They received the document, and during cross-examination, they put one or two questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you the following: A moment ago, in response to my question, you stated that you produced the report on the request of the Prosecution. Answering further to my questions you also said that this was the request of the Defence. And now, in response to my third question, you explained that the Defence counsel did not tell you anything about their requests for the report, and I'd like to know what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is not what the transcript says. And in his response, it says: "On the request of the OTP and in agreement with the Defence in that case, as far as I can remember." If I could also provide some more information, Your Honour, in the trial judgement in the Babic case, the Trial Chamber pointed out that Dr. Loncar, who was called by both parties, testified about his dealings with a large number of war victims. This is in paragraph 52 of the sentencing judgement at the trial stage in the Babic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't understand the story that has to do with the sentencing in the Babic case. I'm trying to identify the task that was given to this man, who gave him that task, and whether this was a joint task of the Prosecution and the Defence, or maybe it was a -- something else. I don't know and it doesn't transpire from the exhibit. And the exhibit was offered to us as a joint task given to the expert by the Prosecution and the Defence in the Babic case. However, all this does not transpire from the document before us or from the answers given so far by the witness, and I don't know why my learned friend objects to any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend was objecting to your characterisation of some of the instructions from the Defence, and she was saying that even the Babic judgement identified the report, the witness's report, as one generated at the request of the Prosecution and the Defence. Be that as it may, I think you have made your point. The only problem that I now have is that you're asking the same questions over and over again and it doesn't make the question any stronger to ask it a second and a third and a fourth time. If you have made it, you've made it, and you can rest assured we've heard it. If you can move on to the next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just a brief question, sir: When you said that Mr. Miller gave -- didn't tell you anything before you embarked on drafting the report - and Mr. Miller was Mr. Babic's Defence lawyer, as far as I know - was that something that said to you that he also wanted to have this report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What was said to me by the OTP, and as far as I could understand it, and it was quite some time ago, was that this was a joint agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another subject. The OTP has provided us with a statement of yours, a witness statement, by Mladen Loncar, with your personal data, the date of birth, the place of birth, the ethnic background, father's name, and it says that you gave that statement on the 25th and 26th October, 2005. This is a statement in which you spoke about Doljani in Jablanica municipality. Can you tell me, what has that got to do with anything that we are talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I don't mention that in my expert report here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that statement of yours, you speak about Croatian victims, and the perpetrators of the crimes were Muslims, the Muslim forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since we don't know where you were born and when, what your father's name is, what your ethnic background or religious affiliation are, let's clarify one thing: The data in that other statement, are they correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to your CV, in answering my learned friend's question, you stated that you graduated in 1987. When did you start studying and where?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I started studying in Novi Sad, and that's where I graduated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In answering my learned friend's question, you also told us that you were born in Bosnia in a small place there, and that at the age of 1 you moved to Ilok, which is a place in Croatia on the very border with Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave for Novi Sad to continue education? Was it before the university or even before that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Before that, I was in Osijek, that's where I attended school. I went to the secondary school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You are a Croat, that's your ethnic background, and in 1981 you moved to Serbia, to Vojvodina, that is, and in Novi Sad you were a medical student and you graduated in 1987. This is all correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours. Before Milosevic came into power, Vojvodina was a beautiful province in Serbia where about 22 different ethnic groups lived happily together, which was often emphasised in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you graduated from the medical school without any problems, you were not discriminated on any grounds?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your CV you say that in 1988 to 1991, you specialised in neuropsychiatry at the Institute for Neurology, Psychiatry and Mental Health of the medical school in Novi Sad and that this specialisation was interrupted by the war. When did this happen? When were you interrupted in your specialisation? What war was the cause of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: This was towards the end of September and beginning of October. This is when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you were detained either in September or October and you established a link between that and the beginning of war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I don't know the -- why I was arrested, but when this happened I asked from the then authorities that had arrested me that I should be tried if I did something wrong, and then they told me that there were no elements for any trial and that I would be transferred to a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This residency that lasted between 1988 and 1991 until the moment you were arrested followed a normal course. There was nothing out of the ordinary with that, and the fact that you had to stop your residency during the war was the arrest. Who were you arrested by?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: It was the province MUP. At that time it was known as SUP, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, towards the end of September or beginning of October, you were -- 1991, you were arrested by the MUP of Serbia. Where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: It happened in a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where was that; in what town?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: It was in Novi Sad, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you were on the way back from somewhere. Where were you before that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you'll allow me, I have to provide a somewhat lengthy answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are allowed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Defence counsel has just said, I grew up in Ilok, which is on the border itself, the border between Croatia and Vojvodina; i.e., Serbia. The distance from Ilok to Novi Sad is about 40 kilometres or half an hour's drive by car. There were no problems there whatsoever, until 1991, when the war started and the easternmost part of Croatia bordering on Vojvodina or Serbia was cut off from the rest of Croatia. The first territorial medical centre that had been established under the then prevailing laws was the hospital in Vukovar. There was heavy fighting going on in the area of Vukovar and neighbouring villages, and an attack was launched from the Sid-Tovarnik-Vukovar axis towards Ilok. The then Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence started occupying one village after another, all of them inhabited by a majority Croatian population. Sometime towards the end of September, beginning of October, the population of Ilok had doubled, or even trebled in that small town, and refugees from the neighbouring villages moved into it. A group of refugees arrived in Ilok, and I remember a man who had survived the execution in Tovarnik. Other refugees brought him to Ilok, and this was the beginning of a humanitarian crisis in this small town which was two or three times bigger than normally, with all the refugees that had arrived there. There was a lack of medical supplies and medicines that were indispensable. Amongst other things, there were no medicines for children. There was at least one child who was on anti-epileptics. This is an indispensable drug that has to be taken continuously. Among those refugees, there was also a lot of wounded civilians who had arrived, and at that moment, I, as a doctor, did what I had to do and what I would always do, regardless of who is in question: I went to buy some drugs, and the only road that was open was the bridge towards Vojvodina, towards Novi Sad. That's where I went to buy some medicines. I went to a pharmacy, I bought the medicines, and on the way back I was arrested in the parking lot and the people who arrested me were MUP members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have provided us with a great detail, describing this period of time. You're talking about the end of September, beginning of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this was on the 1st of October, as far as I can remember. But I must say it was some time ago and I would not dare say that this is the exact date but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My question was not aimed at establishing the exact date. This is not relevant for this part of your testimony. In any case, thank you very much for providing me with all the details. You said that there was war going on around Vukovar, and with this regard I would like to say that on the 26th of June, 1991, five months before that, Croatia had proclaimed its independence from Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I must say that I really don't know. I don't know when this happened. But as far as I know, this was an internationally recognised fact and this was in 1992. At that time, the relevant time, we were still part of the joint state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said "we were part of the joint state." Who is "we" that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: When I say "we" I mean the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbia; i.e., the province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And who was it that waged war in Croatia in September and October, 1991? Whose forces against whose forces?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: As far as I know at the moment - I'm not a lawyer, as you know - but as a human being, what I heard at the moment was there were heavy attacks, there was shelling of Vukovar, the earth was trembling, and during the night it was like fireworks, and the arms --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you be a bit more concise? We are very limited here. I didn't want you to describe the nights in any town of Croatia during fighting. Could you just tell me who the warring parties were in Croatia at the time? Who was fighting whom, if you can? If you can't, just tell us you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What I do know and I am willing to tell you is that the town of Vukovar was defending itself from the attacks by the army and paramilitary formations. As far as I know. I was not in the area, so it's very difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that Vukovar was defending itself from the attacks by the army. Who was it who defended Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there. It's very difficult for me to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've told us one thing now and that is during the time when Croatia was still a part of Yugoslavia, you say we were part of Yugoslavia, the federal army waged a war against somebody who was defending itself from the federal army. Who is it that the federal army was attacking in its own state in 1991? I'm not asking you to answer that, I want to know something else: You said there was a lot of refugees and you say that until the moment you were arrested, you were doing your post-graduate studies in Novi Sad. Are you -- did you go from Novi Sad to Ilok to see what was going on? When did you do that? And then you learned that you had to buy medicines. This is what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that moment, I was on annual leave. I was staying with my parents, with my family, and during my annual leave, the refugees came, and that's when I decided to go and buy some medicines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You know when Croatia was recognised in 1992, but do you know that Croatia proclaimed its secession from Yugoslavia and that's why the war started?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I know that there was a referendum, but I don't know when, what happened, what the legal action was. I really don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We had a witness here who spoke about those events, but let me ask you this: From Ilok, from Croatia, in -- where your parents resided, from the Croatia that had proclaimed its secession from Yugoslavia, it held its referendum, later on was recognised, you returned to Novi Sad, to Serbia, to buy medicines and to bring them back to Croatia, and in such a situation you were arrested by members of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I would like to provide an answer to this question in the following way: At that moment, there were no barriers, there were no borders, there were no customs offices, and I -- Mr. Milosevic had introduced an embargo on the import of products from Slovenia, and I also bought --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're wasting my time. My question to you was as follows: You were in Croatia which had proclaimed its secession from Yugoslavia. It was in the state of war. You went to Serbia to buy drugs and then you were arrested by the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you charged with buying medical supplies for the enemy in the war, the other side in the war, where you intended to take those materials? Were you charged with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you charged with having stolen those medical supplies in the medical centre where you worked at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: No. If I may, Your Honour, I can tell you what the charges were, actually what they were questioning me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir. You may do that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: When I was arrested, they started questioning me about the military structures and forces, and I didn't have a clue about all that, because in Ilok, at that moment, there were only refugees and expelled persons, and this is what they wanted to know, all they wanted to know from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You state that you were arrested in late October, early November. Before that, in this non-democratic Vojvodina, as you explained it was because of Milosevic's rule, you established a Croatian party and you were a member of its leadership; isn't that correct? When did this take place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not set up a party. Rather, I set up a branch office of a party. This took place in 1990, after the democratic change, when a multi-party system was introduced, and when political parties were being set up. I decided to set up a branch office in Novi Sad, and the sole aim was to organise the national minority and develop the cultural institutions of the minority. Literally speaking, in this Vojvodina, which was a multi-ethnic community, ethnically tolerant, we wanted to have the Croatian national minority develop and strive -- and thrive as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in Vojvodina, you set up a party in 1991. What was the name of the party?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't establish a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. The branch office.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The party was called the Democratic Alliance of Croats in Vojvodina. The party was already in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you stated that it was in early 1990, at the time of democratic change and the introduction of a multi-party system, you set up a party belonging to the Croatian national minority in Vojvodina, which I have no problem with. Do you know who was the president of Serbia at the time? Was it Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Again, I did not set up a political party but, rather, its branch office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I made the same mistake for the third time. I apologise. At the time, in a multi-ethnic Vojvodina, where there were many national minorities and there were many political parties, you set up a branch office of this national minority's party. Where was its seat?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: In Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what were you there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I was the head of the branch office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And do you consider the conditions for the establishment of branch office as non-democratic and unfriendly? Was Mr. Milosevic president of Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that after your arrest, you ended up in a centre which is called Begejci. Who ran the centre and what sort of a centre was it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I have to say first that before that I was taken to another centre which was called Paragovo, which was held by the JNA at the time. After that, I was transferred to the Begejci camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who ran this Begejci camp, and how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The camp was ran by the JNA, at least formally, according to what it said, but it was manned by members of the MUP from Serbia. I believe I spent a bit over a month in this camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well, am I right in saying that the Begejci camp was an institution run by the Yugoslav People's Army? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, when Croatia was part of Yugoslavia, the JNA was the federal armed force, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You authored several reports and studies, some of them are even included in your CV, where you state that you were in the Serb camp of Begejci. How can an institution under the jurisdiction of the JNA be called a Serb camp, as you call it, or do you have something against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to clarify any imputations to me. I have many friends among the Serbs. The fact of the matter is at the time when I was brought to the camp, which had all the attributes of a concentration camp - I did write about that - there were mostly civilians there, the elderly, the infirm and children, and I don't know whose enemies they could have been. They were elderly people, above 70 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the Begejci camp, you mentioned the Sremska Mitrovica camp and the one at Stajici [phoen]. Are you familiar with those?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. I learned about these camps from victims, and I wrote about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, you call all of these institutions camps. You even go so far as to say that they were concentration camps, whereas the Amnesty International report dated March, 1992, for Yugoslavia, speaks of JNA camps, or even JNA centres at Stajicevo, Begejci, and about the prison at Sremska Mitrovica. Do you draw any distinctions between the collection centre, temporary centre, and prison, and a concentration camp on the other?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Of course I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should break for the day -- oh, no we still have 15 minutes left. I was mistaken. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: After I was brought to this collection centre, as you call it, and on the basis of what I knew about human rights and the international norms related to human rights - and this was part of my general knowledge, I didn't have any legal training - you can call it whatever you like, but this was the sort of camp where civilians were brought to without any charges having been brought against them, without any convictions passed, only because on some basis they were different from others. They were brought over from Croatia. Now that you mentioned secession - I'm using your term, the term that you used - I got there before the JNA took Vukovar, seized Vukovar, and the guards who were there said, as far as we were able to hear, that the camp's main purpose was to bring over Ustashas, as they put it, from Vukovar. I don't know what sort of army it was, whether it was really a people's army. It used to be, unfortunately, but that's why I called those camps as concentration camps, because people brought over there were brought there only because their affiliations lay elsewhere or because they were members of different ethnicities, although among them there were also Serbs who, for one or -- reason or the other did not wish to embrace such ideas. As a result, I can say that the camp was, as far as I was able to see at the time, mostly populated with citizens from Croatia, although there were people brought over from other republics, which were not engaged in any fighting, as far as I know, and all the inmates were subjected to the same type of torture. None of us were ever part of any legal proceedings. We didn't know the charges against us, if any, and that's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Milovancevic. You had said before, Doctor, that the camps had the characteristics, all the characteristics of a concentration camp. Now, other than the features which you referred to immediately in your evidence concerning why you say it is a concentration-type camp, do you have any other characteristics other than those characteristics which would have identified them to you as concentration camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the reasons why I characterised the camp as such are as follows: As according to their structure, these camps were set up like the concentration camps I was able to see from World War II. The camps had two rings of barbed wire around them, between the two rings of barbed wire, the Alsatian German shepherd dogs were placed. There were armed guards there, and in the inner ring, the inner ring was manned by the camp staff. Now, the second reason I called it that way was that the inmates were mostly civilians of an advanced age. In my assessment there were about 500 to 600 of us. We were all housed in one barn, lying on the bare floor, on the concrete ground, which only had some straw strewn about it. In Vojvodina, temperatures at the time would go below ten degrees Celsius below zero. The third reason why I characterised the camps as concentration camps was that the people were taken there without any prior convictions, merely -- it was merely driven by the will of the law enforcement agency. People were taken there against their own will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another thing, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One other feature was that there was systematic torture applied. There were every day beatings, starvation, groups of people were taken out without ever having been taken back, and later on it turned out that they were executed. These were the reasons, Your Honour, why I characterised these venues as concentration camps. I'm not a lawyer, but based on my general knowledge, I feel free enough to describe them as such. One more sentence, Your Honours: There were women there. I believe that there were about 30 of them. From conversations with these women later on, I knew that many of them were victims of rape and had gone through horrific torture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the explanation you gave the Honourable Judge Nosworthy, do you know what the general definition of a concentration camp is? Simply the fascist factory of death, where millions of people ended up. And do you know that the only concentration camp with such hallmarks, and even worse ones, existed only in the Republic of Croatia, at Jasenovac, where 700.000 people were killed. Their throats were slit. Do you distinguish between such different types of institutions or are you simply taking concentration camps in -- not seriously? Do you know that there were only 500 people in -- that the camp was disbanded in late 1991, according to one person's report?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. I think the witness has been asked the question as to what his -- what he meant and he answered it. He answered what he meant by the use of the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just suggested to the witness, who should know that because he's an educated man, what the real meaning of the term "concentration camp" is. The explanation provided to the Trial Chamber is just mockery, mocking the Jewish victims and other victims of real concentration camps. 500 people in an improvised camp that the Amnesty International describes in 1992, he believes that this was a concentration camp, and I just wanted to know whether he made any distinction, and that's what I based my question on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milovancevic, I think the question you had asked the witness, and he gave -- actually, you didn't ask the question, Judge Nosworthy asked the question, and the witness gave a very lengthy explanation of what made him characterise those camps as concentration camps. You either believe him or you don't believe him. And if you don't believe him, you tell him why you don't believe him. But I think to suggest that his answer is a mockery and a mocking of the Jewish victims. He has hardly said a word about Jewish victims. I think you're taking it very far, Mr. Milovancevic. The fact that he's an educated person doesn't mean he's a know-all, but he's given his explanation to the best of his ability, and you stay within that and accept it or tell him that you don't believe him if you don't believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept your suggestion, Your Honour, and thank you for your instruction. I shall withdraw the last part of my question and I'm going to ask Mr. Loncar the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the term "concentration camp" was something that was used for fascist factories of death, that were used for the systematic daily extermination of hundreds of thousands of people? Do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, I'm going to have to disallow that question. The witness has told you, or has told the Chamber what he understood the camps that he described as concentration camps to be, and he said he understood them to be like that because of the characteristics that he gave us. Now, once you start talking of fascists and you are going into history which is not part of this case, which is not before this case, and I think you are bringing in very emotional characterisations of the issues here, and I would expect you, as an officer of the Court, to keep your cool and ask questions. Now, this -- ask questions and stop making suggestions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that a majority of the people in the Begejci camp, in the camp under the control of the JNA, were Croats. Do you have any knowledge as to the fact that during the year 1991, there had been an armed rebellion in Croatia? The Prosecution witness Maksic testified to that. This armed rebellion involved a lot of Croats against the federal state. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge about that in the way your question has been worded. I would not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that Vukovar and other places in Croatia were defending themselves against a federal army. Who was involved in that defence; Croatian army, civilians, who?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: There is a major difference between defending oneself and being engaged in a rebellion, and I get your point. What happened in Vukovar was defence. Vukovar was defending itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've explained that in Croatia in 1991, there was fighting and is there any doubt that there were two sides to that fighting? One side was the armed forces of Yugoslavia and the other side the Croatian authorities with its armed formations and the population of Croatia? Do you doubt that? Is there anything in dispute about that in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Partially, yes. The way you are wording your questions, I'm tempted to say that partially you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Can you be -- repeat your question? And what is it that you're asking me exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It was not my intention not to be clear, however, my intention backfired. In Croatia -- in the territory of Croatia, in 1991, was there a conflict between the federal armed forces and the Croatian armed forces of the new Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. There was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any people taken prisoner during those fightings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The new armed forces comprised of Croats, mostly of Croats?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: This makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Will it then make sense that the prisoners from the new ranks of Croatian army were also Croats?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your logic is partly okay but the other part is not okay, because there were civilians. What did they have to do with the army? What does a grandmother aged 80, or a child, have to do with that? Why were they in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will establish that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that we have reached the end of the day. I would like to thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. The Court will adjourn and we will resume tomorrow afternoon at quarter past 2.00. The Court will adjourn now. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
